## Question 1

## Question 2

.font120[Which of the following is usually the MOST reliable for accurate scientific information?]

.font110[
A. Wikipedia &nbsp;&nbsp; B. TikTok video &nbsp;&nbsp; C. Peer-reviewed science journal &nbsp;&nbsp; D. Reddit post
]

--

.font150[`r fontawesome::fa("check", fill = "#009E73")` **Answer: C**]

---
class: center, middle

## Question 3

.font120[What should you check to see if a website is trustworthy?]

.font110[
A. Its color and design &nbsp;&nbsp; B. If it has ads <br>

]

--

.font150[`r fontawesome::fa("check", fill = "#009E73")` **Answer: C**]

class: center, middle

.font120[Which source is the least likely to be biased?]

.font100[
A. A product review written by the company that made the product <br>
B. A university study published in a journal <br>
C. A celebrity's opinion on a diet trend <br>
D. A tweet from a random user
]

.font150[`r fontawesome::fa("check", fill = "#009E73")` **Answer: B**]

### Refresher: Reliable vs. Unreliable Sources

.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
### `r fontawesome::fa("circle-check", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Reliable Sources

- Backed by verifiable evidence
- Created by experts
- Undergo review processes
- Transparent about methods
- Cite their sources
]
]

.pull-right[
.content-box-yellow[
### `r fontawesome::fa("triangle-exclamation", height = "1em")` Unreliable Sources

- Lack transparency
- Anonymous or unclear authorship
- Sensationalist language
- One-sided arguments
- Missing citations
]
]

### Refresher: Red Flags of Misinformation

.pull-left[
```{r img1, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="58%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/01-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

.pull-right[
#### `r fontawesome::fa("bullhorn", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Sensational Language
"You won't believe this!" or excessive punctuation for shock value.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("user-slash", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Missing Attribution
No clear author, source, or supporting evidence.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("scale-unbalanced", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; One-Sided Presentation
No acknowledgment of alternative perspectives or debates.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("wand-sparkles", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Extraordinary Claims
Bold statements without proportional evidence.
]

### Observation: Watching Real Behavior

.pull-left[
```{r img6, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="58%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/06-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

.pull-right[.font90[
#### `r fontawesome::fa("tree", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Natural Settings
Observe behavior as it naturally occurs without intervention.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("list-check", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Structured or Unstructured
Use checklists for specific behaviors or take open-ended notes on everything you see.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("clock", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Time Sampling
Observe at different times to capture variation in behavior patterns.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("user-secret", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Minimize Observer Effect
Be discreet so your presence doesn't change the behavior you're studying.

*Can be utilized in quantitative or qualitative studies.*
]]

---
### Case Studies: Deep Dives

.pull-left[
```{r img7, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="58%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/07-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

.pull-right[.font90[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("book", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Definition**

Intensive study of a single case or small number of cases to gain in-depth understanding.
]

.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("circle-check", fill = "#4a7fb5")` When to Use**

For unique situations, rare phenomena, or when you need comprehensive understanding of one example.
]

.content-box-yellow[
**`r fontawesome::fa("triangle-exclamation", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Limitations**

Findings may not generalize to other cases or populations.
]

*Mostly qualitative but can include quantitative elements*
]]

---
### Using Existing Data: Secondary Research

.pull-left[
```{r img8, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="58%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/08-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

.pull-right[
#### `r fontawesome::fa("bolt", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Efficient Access
Use data already collected by others instead of gathering new information.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("landmark", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Historical Perspective
Analyze trends over time periods you couldn't study directly.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("database", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Multiple Sources
Government reports, research studies, archives, statistics, and historical documents.

#### `r fontawesome::fa("magnifying-glass", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` &nbsp; Source Verification
Always evaluate the credibility and quality of secondary data sources.
]

---
### Mixed Methods: Combining Approaches & Tools

.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("star", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Benefits**

- Provides fuller picture of the topic
- Combines breadth and depth
- Numbers + stories = comprehensive understanding
- Compensates for weaknesses in single methods
]
]

.pull-right[
.content-box-green[
**`r fontawesome::fa("puzzle-piece", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Examples**

- Survey + interviews
- Experiment + questionnaire
- Observation + focus groups
- Case study + statistical analysis
]
]

<div style="clear: both;"></div>

.center[Mixed methods require careful planning but provide **rich, multidimensional insights**.]

### Choosing the Right Method

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">1</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Consider your research question</strong><br>
  What type of answer do you need? Numbers, descriptions, or both?</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">2</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Assess your resources</strong><br>
  How much time, access, and materials do you have available?</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">3</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Think about participants</strong><br>
  Who will you study and how many can you realistically include?</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">4</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Weigh strengths and limitations</strong><br>
  Each method has trade-offs. Choose what best fits your specific needs.</div>
</div>

---
### Correlation vs. Causation

.pull-left[
.content-box-blue[
### `r fontawesome::fa("arrows-left-right", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Correlation

Two variables change together or are related.

- Shows a pattern or relationship
- Doesn't prove one causes the other
- Found in surveys, observations, etc.
]
]

.pull-right[
.content-box-green[
### `r fontawesome::fa("arrow-right", height = "1em", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Causation

One variable directly causes changes in another.

- Shows cause and effect
- Requires controlled experiments
- Harder to establish definitively
]
]

<div style="clear: both;"></div>

.center[**Remember:** "Correlation does not equal causation" is a fundamental principle in research.]

### Planning the Procedure

<div class="chev-flow">
  <div class="chev-step">
    <div class="chev-right">`r fontawesome::fa("file-pen", height = "1.6em", fill = "#0148A4")`</div>
    <p><strong>Write Clear Instructions</strong><br>
    Create a detailed "recipe" for your research that someone else could follow.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="chev-step">
    <div class="chev-right">`r fontawesome::fa("sliders", height = "1.6em", fill = "#0148A4")`</div>
    <p><strong>Consider All Variables</strong><br>
    Identify what you'll change, what you'll measure, and what you'll keep constant.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="chev-step">
    <div class="chev-right">`r fontawesome::fa("table-list", height = "1.6em", fill = "#0148A4")`</div>
    <p><strong>Plan Data Collection</strong><br>
    Decide exactly what data you'll gather and how you'll record it.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="chev-step">
    <div class="chev-right">`r fontawesome::fa("triangle-exclamation", height = "1.6em", fill = "#0148A4")`</div>
    <p><strong>Anticipate Challenges</strong><br>
    Think about what might go wrong and how you'll handle it.</p>
  </div>
</div>
]

---
### Experiment Procedure Planning

.pull-left[
```{r img13, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="58%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/13-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

.pull-right[.font90[
<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">1</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Define Your Groups</strong><br>
  Decide who or what will be in experimental and control groups. Use random assignment when possible.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">2</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Define the Treatment</strong><br>
  Clearly describe what you'll do with the experimental group. Be specific enough for replication.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">3</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Define Control Activities</strong><br>
  Decide what the control group will do during the same time period.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">4</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Plan Data Collection</strong><br>
  Determine exactly what measurements you'll take, when, and how.</div>
</div>
]]

---
### Survey Procedure Planning

.pull-left[
```{r img14, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="58%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/14-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

.pull-right[.font90[
<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">1</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Distribution Method</strong><br>
  Decide how to give out your survey: paper, online, in-person. Each has pros and cons for reach and response rate.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">2</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Target Respondents</strong><br>
  Define who should take your survey. Aim for a representative sample, not just friends.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">3</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Question Design</strong><br>
  Write clear, unbiased questions. Test them on a few people first to check for confusion.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">4</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Response Collection</strong><br>
  Plan how to gather and analyze answers. Set a timeline with reminders for participants.</div>
</div>
]]

---
### Observation Procedure Planning

.pull-left[
```{r img15, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.width=4, fig.height=6, out.width="58%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/15-img.png")

# Plot the image
grid.raster(img)
```
]

.pull-right[.font90[
<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">1</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Choose Locations and Times</strong><br>
  Create a clear schedule for when and where you'll observe. Include multiple times to identify patterns.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">2</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Define Observation Focus</strong><br>
  Decide exactly what behaviors or phenomena you'll look for to stay organized.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">3</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Plan to Minimize Influence</strong><br>
  Be discreet so your presence doesn't change the behavior you're studying.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">4</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Create Recording Method</strong><br>
  Decide how you'll document observations: tally sheet, notes, sketches, or digital tools.</div>
</div>
]]

---
### Using Existing Data: Procedure Planning

.pull-left[

]

.pull-right[.font90[
<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">1</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Identify Sources</strong><br>
  Make a list of all data sources you plan to use, like databases, archives, or publications.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">2</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Verify Credibility</strong><br>
  Check that sources are trustworthy, like government agencies, universities, or reputable organizations.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">3</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Plan Data Extraction</strong><br>
  Decide what specific information you need from each source and how you'll organize it.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">4</div>
  <div class="chev-text"><strong>Organize Information</strong><br>
  Create a system to track where each piece of data came from and how it relates to your question.</div>
</div>
]]

### Hands-On Mini Experiment: Chewing Gum &amp; Memory

.content-box-yellow[
**`r fontawesome::fa("circle-question", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Research Question:** "Does chewing gum improve short-term memory in middle and high school students?"
]

.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("lightbulb", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Hypothesis (Testable Statement):** "Students who chew gum will remember more words from a list than students who don't."
]

--

#### So let's think about what kind of data we can work with: Qualitative vs Quantitative?

#### And how can we go about collecting our data to test our very testable statement, aka our hypothesis?

---
### Hands-On Mini Experiment: Chewing Gum &amp; Memory

**Experiment Steps:**

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">1</div>
  <div class="chev-text">Here is a list of <strong>10 simple words</strong>.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">2</div>
  <div class="chev-text">We are to <strong>randomly divide</strong> you all into two groups (chewing gum vs. no gum).</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">3</div>
  <div class="chev-text">You will <strong>see the list for 30 seconds</strong>. Then we will wait for 1 minute. Then you will write as many words as you can remember.</div>
</div>

<div class="chev-row">
  <div class="chev">4</div>
  <div class="chev-text">That would allow us to <strong>compare average number of words recalled</strong> per group.</div>
</div>

---
### Chewing Gum &amp; Memory: Research Design Discussion

.pull-left[.font90[
.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("sliders", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Independent variable:** Gum or no gum
]

.content-box-blue[
**`r fontawesome::fa("gauge-high", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Dependent variable:** Number of words remembered
]

.content-box-green[
**`r fontawesome::fa("lock", fill = "#4a7fb5")` Control variables:** Word list, exposure time, wait time before recall, setting
]
]]

.pull-right[
```{r img25, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center'}
# Read the image file
img <- readPNG("assets/25-img.png")

# Plot the image

```

**Could the results support or refute the hypothesis? What might influence that outcome?**

*e.g., nerves, distractions, small sample size*
]
]
